# Gengchou v2.5.2

v2.5.2 is a fix release, and most of it is Gengchou stopping without telling
you. A panic on a background thread left the usage frozen for as long as the
app stayed open; a settings file that could not be read was replaced by
defaults within seconds of launch; a provider that answered with an empty quota
window had its numbers erased and the refresh recorded as a success; a second
signed-in Windows account got no window at all. None of these announced
themselves, which is what they have in common and why they are grouped here.
The rest of the release hardens the updater against being pointed somewhere it
does not belong.

The executable, settings-directory, cache, and update identities are unchanged.
One internal name did change: the single-instance lock, which is now derived
from the data directory rather than being machine-wide. Nothing outside the app
reads that name.

## Changes

- Let a second Windows account run Gengchou. The single-instance lock was
  machine-wide while settings and the usage cache are per user, so two accounts
  that share no file still excluded each other - and the second one's launch
  ended with no window, no tray icon and no message. The lock is now scoped to
  the data directory it protects, so two accounts never collide and two
  sessions of one account still do. A launch that cannot start either brings
  the existing window forward or says why.
- Keep polling after a background thread fails. A panic on the poll worker or
  the credential watch left the flag that says "one pass is already running"
  set for the rest of the process's life, so every later refresh was folded
  into a pending pass that nobody ran. The usage froze at the last good values
  while the window, the tray and the menus all kept working normally - the only
  trace was a line in the diagnostic log. Both flags are now released even when
  the pass comes apart, so the next scheduled refresh starts a fresh worker.
- Keep the numbers on screen when a provider answers with nothing. Claude and
  Codex treated an HTTP 200 that carried no usable quota window as a successful
  refresh with an empty result. Because an empty result is drawn exactly like
  "no data", the visible outcome was that your usage disappeared while the
  status line said it had just been updated, and the previous values were
  discarded rather than kept. Both now treat that answer as a failed refresh:
  the last good numbers stay, marked stale. Antigravity and Grok already
  behaved this way.
- Keep a settings file that cannot be read. Returning to defaults was never
  read-only: the defaults carry no consent decision and no update-check
  timestamp, so the first-run prompt and an update check both ran and both
  saved, replacing your layout, language, provider selection and access
  decisions within seconds. The unreadable file is now kept as
  `settings.json.corrupt` before defaults load, and one warning names that
  path. A single generation is kept, and the original is never deleted - if it
  cannot be preserved, that is reported rather than passed over.
- Survive an Explorer restart when the process-level helper could not be
  created at startup. In that fallback the taskbar widget also owns the poll
  timer, the credential watch and the periodic provider sweep, and Windows
  delivers a timer only to the window it was set on - so all three died with
  the widget Explorer destroyed and nothing re-armed them on its replacement.
  Monitoring stopped for good, quietly. The session-notification registration
  was lost the same way.
- Confirm a completed update before anything can wait on you. The updater gives
  a new build 30 seconds to report that it started healthily and otherwise
  rolls back to the previous version, and that confirmation used to come after
  two dialogs that can sit on screen indefinitely: the first-run access prompt,
  and the storage warning raised when the last save failed. An update that
  arrived alongside either one was rolled back while the dialog was still open.
- Stop a reset notification from being raised while the shared application
  state is locked. The notification call reaches Explorer synchronously and
  Explorer can call straight back into Gengchou's window procedure, which needs
  that same lock - a hang with the interface and the poll thread each waiting
  on the other. The three other notification sites already released the lock
  first.
- Read a settings file written by a newer build instead of rejecting it. A
  window position, floating position, or last-update result recorded in a form
  this build has never seen used to fail the whole file. Only the field that
  cannot be represented is dropped now, and the rest of the file is kept.
- Scope the diagnostic log's cross-process lock to the log file. The log lives
  under `%LOCALAPPDATA%` and is therefore per user, while the lock was
  machine-wide, so unrelated accounts on the same machine waited on each
  other's writes.
- Start Windows programs by absolute path. `wsl.exe`, `powershell.exe` and
  `where.exe` were named plainly, and Windows resolves a plain name against the
  running program's own directory before the system directory - so a file with
  one of those names sitting next to a portable `gengchou.exe`, which normally
  lives in a downloads folder, would have been run instead. `wsl.exe` is what
  reads credentials from a WSL distribution and `powershell.exe` is what drives
  a WinGet update. The Claude CLI used for the optional
  `--claude-auth-diagnostics` report is now located the same way the automatic
  `claude update` already located it.
- Read a credential probe's answer while it is still running. Waiting for the
  process to exit before reading its output deadlocks any child that writes
  more than the pipe buffer holds: it blocks mid-write, the timeout expires,
  and an ordinary answer that was merely large is reported as a provider that
  never responded. A timeout now also ends the whole process tree; the Claude
  CLI is normally a `claude.cmd` shim, so stopping only the shim left the work
  running past the deadline that was supposed to stop it.
- Say when diagnostic logging could not be started. That failure was discarded,
  and every later log call - including the panic hook - silently does nothing
  once it happens, so the app ran with no record of anything and no explanation
  for the missing file.
- Refuse an update that is not this installation. `--apply-update` took a
  target path and a source path and replaced one with the other, with nothing
  requiring the target to be the app that started it. It now proves that from
  the parent process's image path, or from the updater's own bytes when the
  parent has already exited, and refuses rather than replacing or launching
  anything else.
- Check the download's version, not only its hash. A hash proves the file is
  the one `SHA256SUMS` names; it says nothing about which build that file is.
  The WinGet path has always compared `ProductVersion` after upgrading, and the
  portable path now compares it before installing.
- Check the updater's own working directory before downloading into it. That
  directory is emptied, downloaded into, and then executed out of, but the
  reparse-point check ran only later, inside the helper - after a redirected
  directory had already received both the download and a copy of the app.

## Not changed

- Vertical taskbars remain unsupported, and the README now says so. The widget
  is laid out along a horizontal bar and is wider than a left- or right-docked
  taskbar; the floating window and the tray icons work there.

## Updating

No settings or cache migration is required, and no re-authorization is needed.
Users of v2.5.1 can update normally.

Because the single-instance lock is named differently, this build and a v2.5.1
or earlier build do not recognize each other through it. Updating replaces the
old build before the new one starts, so this does not arise there; launching
both by hand during the changeover is the one case where two copies could run
at once, and the second launch still defers to a Gengchou window already open
on the same desktop.

One consequence of scoping the lock per data directory: if you keep a single
copy of `gengchou.exe` in a folder shared by several accounts, two of them can
now have it running at the same time. A self-update started by one of them
while another is running that same file fails and rolls back - Windows will not
replace a loaded image - rather than corrupting anything.

Downgrading to v2.5.1 or earlier is safe for the settings this release writes,
with one exception that only applies later: from this release onward, a
placement or last-update value that an older build cannot read costs that one
field instead of the whole settings file. Older builds do not have that
tolerance, so if a future release introduces such a value, downgrading past
this one would still reset your settings.

Do not update an installation older than v2.2.4 directly to this release. Keep
and run the v2.2.4 bridge build twice first, confirm the migration, and only
then move to v2.3.0 or later.
